paragraphs: Friend, here's what I take from this one. Before a single sword comes out, God settles who the army is counting on. When Israel sees horses, chariots and a bigger army, Moses says, "do not be afraid of them; for the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, is with you" (Deuteronomy 20:1). The priest repeats it before the battle: the LORD your God "goes with you to fight for you against your enemies, to give you the victory" (Deuteronomy 20:4).

Now notice how much care is packed into these laws. A man who built a new house and hasn't dedicated it, planted a vineyard and hasn't begun to enjoy its fruit, or is pledged to a woman and hasn't married her is sent home (Deuteronomy 20:5-7), and so is any man who is afraid, so that "the hearts of his brothers will not melt like his own" (Deuteronomy 20:8). A far-off city gets an offer of peace first (Deuteronomy 20:10), and even the fruit trees are protected, with Moses asking, "Are the trees of the field human, that you should besiege them?" (Deuteronomy 20:19). I think the words about the nations God is giving Israel are heavy, and Moses gives the reason: so they cannot teach Israel "all the detestable things they do for their gods," and lead Israel into sinning against the LORD (Deuteronomy 20:16-18).

So what do you do with that, baker? When you face something bigger than you, you don't count your own strength first. You start with who is standing beside you, and then you move with care. And Moses isn't done preaching yet, so keep listening.
